items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: Never met Cannonball. No, never met him.

ctx.x: I see. Well thank you for sharing that with me. I wanted to go back to this, I heard you and Murray Horwitz on the air, a re-play of one of the albums you picked for that marvelous jazz review and it was Cannonball and “Something Else.” And on the “Autumn Leaves” you called his solo “perfect, not a wrong note.” And I’m a huge Cannonball fan so it really caught my attention. And it’s been a while but can you recall why you felt it was perfect?

Why I felt it was perfect. Well Cannonball had a gift for connecting his notes in such a way that every one seemed like the right note. Now some other people like, again, Coletrane again would be more like challenging with the way his notes related to each other. He would create all these tensions within his music and even use things like quarter tones to challenge your ear a bit more. So the sense of rightness that this is the correct note doesn’t come into it in the same way that it would with Cannonball. With…

everything that had gone before it. And so that was a great gift of Cannonball’s. He did this time after time after time, I mean that everything seemed to flow very very logically out of everything else. And it made his solos appear like organic, like little bodies of things. And also he had just such a beautiful sound, just a perfect, perfect casual way of phrasing, playing very difficult passages as if they were just the easiest things in the world to express. I had a great admiration for his music.
